passages.t: Exile, and the people who came home
passages.happening:
‘So all Israel was recorded in the genealogies written in the Book of the Kings of Israel. But Judah was exiled to Babylon because of their unfaithfulness’ (verse 1).

Then: ‘Now the first to resettle their own property in their cities were Israelites, priests, Levites, and temple servants’ (verse 2). People from Judah, Benjamin, Ephraim and Manasseh live in Jerusalem (verse 3), and their families are listed (verses 4-9). The priests follow, among them Azariah, ‘the chief official of God’s temple’ (verse 11), and the Levites (verses 14-16).
passages.hearers:
Eight chapters of names have covered every tribe. Verse 1 draws a line under them and names the disaster in one sentence. Then the Chronicler turns at once to the people who came back, which is where his readers lived. Placing this list right after ancient Israel's tells the community that they are the continuation of the whole story.

The word for unfaithfulness, ma'al, is the Chronicler's summary of Israel's sin: a betrayal of trust in a covenant. In this same chapter the gatekeepers are appointed to positions of emunah, faithfulness. A people exiled for unfaithfulness is restored through faithful service.

People from Ephraim and Manasseh, northern tribes, also lived in Jerusalem after the exile. Most read verse 2 as describing the first returnees after Cyrus's decree of 539 or 538 BC. The temple servants, in Hebrew netinim, those given, helped the Levites with manual work; they appear among the returnees in Ezra.
passages.later: Nehemiah tells how ‘the leaders of the people settled in Jerusalem, and the rest of the people cast lots to bring one out of ten to live in the holy city of Jerusalem’ (Nehemiah 11:1).
passages.hard:
Why does the list of Jerusalem's residents differ from the similar list in Nehemiah 11?

The two lists overlap a great deal but are not identical. They share names such as Sallu, Jedaiah, Jachin, Adaiah, Shemaiah son of Hasshub, Mattaniah son of Mica, Akkub and Talmon, but they differ in some names and numbers. The leading man of Judah is Uthai here and Athaiah in Nehemiah; the chief official of God's house is Azariah son of Hilkiah here and Seraiah son of Hilkiah there; there are 956 Benjaminites here and 928 there; and only Chronicles mentions residents from Ephraim and Manasseh. Scholars offer several explanations. Some think both lists draw on a common record, which each writer adapted. Others think they describe different moments in the resettlement. Differences in copying names and numbers are also possible. The lists agree on the main point: after the exile, families from Judah and Benjamin, with priests and Levites, came back to Jerusalem and restored its life and worship.
passages.asks: The genealogies end with exile and then turn at once to those who came home. Ask what in your life has been lost through unfaithfulness, and what God might be restoring. And ask where you belong in the story of God's people now.

passages.happening:
The gatekeepers are named (verses 17-21). ‘The number of those chosen to be gatekeepers at the thresholds was 212’ (verse 22), and ‘David and Samuel the seer had appointed them to their positions of trust’ (verse 22). They guard all four sides (verse 24), and relatives come in from the villages to serve for seven days at a time (verse 25). The four chief gatekeepers are entrusted with the rooms and treasuries, and they ‘would spend the night stationed around the house of God, because they were responsible for guarding it and opening it every morning’ (verse 27).

Other Levites count the vessels in and out, keep the flour, wine, oil, frankincense and spices, bake the offering bread and prepare the bread set out each Sabbath (verses 28-32). The musicians stay in the temple chambers, ‘because they were on duty day and night’ (verse 33). The chapter ends by repeating the family of Saul (verses 35-44).
passages.hearers:
The temple was a place of sacrifice, but also a treasury, a storehouse and a holy precinct that had to be guarded against theft and against anyone entering where they should not. Gatekeepers were more than doormen. They were responsible for the holiness and safety of the sanctuary. Their office is traced back to Phinehas, Aaron's grandson, and to the arrangements of David and Samuel; the Chronicler presents the second temple's staff as heirs of an order that ran back to Israel's beginnings.

The bread set out each Sabbath, twelve loaves, stood for the twelve tribes always before God. Service rotated: relatives came in from the villages for a week, which let families farm their land and still serve. The musicians were on duty day and night.

The long description slows the story down, lingering on the care of God's house. The repeated list of Saul's family brings the reader to the door of chapter 10, where the story of the kingdom begins.
passages.later: The law said, ‘Every Sabbath day the bread is to be set out before the LORD on behalf of the Israelites as a permanent covenant’ (Leviticus 24:8). A psalm says, ‘I would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God than dwell in the tents of the wicked’ (Psalm 84:10).
passages.asks: Gatekeepers stayed up all night and opened the house every morning. Ask what quiet, faithful work keeps your church or your home open. And ask whether you would count it a privilege to be a doorkeeper in God's house.
